title: Science close

segments.voice: Yesterday: your own experiment, Franklin's little book with a page for each virtue. Your line was my experiment. Did you write the first entry? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

For ninety days this path has been living in the lab. Meditators and scientists at one table. A gorilla people missed. A habit curve that forgives a missed day. A stranger on crutches in a waiting room, seminary students in a hurry, a nerve with too many promises hung on it. Then a long, uncomfortable stretch on studies that didn't hold up. Today the lab door closes, and the question is simple: what do you carry out, and how tightly do you hold it?
screen: `NINETY DAYS IN THE LAB.` → `GORILLAS, HABITS, HURRY, NERVES.` → `WHAT DO YOU CARRY OUT?`

segments.voice: First, the four rooms. This block ran through attention, then habit, then compassion, then the honest part: replication, placebo, sleep, money, purpose and the edge of what can be measured. Second, two piles. Some findings held up well across studies and are worth building on: attention is limited, habits take shape slowly and survive a missed day, slow breathing can settle the body, kindness can be practiced. Other claims stayed shaky: single studies never repeated, popular stories that ran ahead of their data, big promises about one nerve or one hormone. The skill wasn't memorizing which pile. It was learning to ask, each time, how big is the claim, and how strong is the evidence? Third, two old voices that asked the same thing. In the Buddhist Kalama Sutta, the Buddha tells the Kalamas, townspeople confused by rival teachers, not to accept something just because of tradition, report or a teacher's authority, but to take it up when they know for themselves it leads to good. And Paul writes to the church at Thessalonica, in the King James Bible: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Different traditions, a shared habit: test, then hold. Fourth, the shape of it. Hold the solid things firmly enough to practice them every day. Hold the rest lightly, open to being wrong. Tomorrow the path leaves the lab for the world's schools of practice, starting with Zen. Solid and light.
screen: `ATTENTION, HABIT, COMPASSION, HONESTY.` · `WHAT HELD UP, AND WHAT STAYED SHAKY.` · `KNOW FOR YOURSELVES; PROVE ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `HOLD FAST WHAT IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep what's solid, hold the rest lightly. Sit comfortably and breathe. Open both hands on your knees, palms up. In the right hand, place one thing from these ninety days you're keeping for good: a practice, or a finding you trust. Feel it there, steady. In the left hand, place one claim you're no longer sure of. Don't throw it away. Just let it rest there, open. Breathe between the two. If you pray, you can offer both hands as they are. The bell holds the time.
Science close. Ninety days through attention, habit, compassion and the honest part, and one habit to keep: test, then hold. A week and a block end here. Today's word.
Your line: solid and light. Today, tell one person the one thing you're keeping from these ninety days, and the one you're holding loosely. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: People who draw on both science and tradition often keep practices with solid evidence as daily habits, while holding newer or single-study claims loosely until they're tested again.

fork.setup: a new single study goes viral: a practice rewires your brain in a week. after ninety days of honest science, what do you do?
options: decide all science is hype and ignore it.
try the practice if it helps, and hold the claim lightly until it's tested again.
fork.reveal: that's the habit of this block, and an old one: "prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

trapdoor: what you thought: science either proves a practice works or it doesn't.
what it means: some findings are solid enough to build on; others are shaky and held lightly.
what a scholar hears: evidence comes in degrees: replication, effect size and study design decide how firmly a claim deserves to be held.
